extracted.intended_audience: students, general readers, and scholars researching F. Scott Fitzgerald and his fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Critical/biographical overview of F. Scott Fitzgerald's themes, style, criticism, influence, and adaptations, useful for literary analysis or contextualizing creative-writing practices derived from his work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of American class system
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald's characters are trapped in a rigid American class system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fiction foregrounds status anxieties and social conflict arising from entrenched prejudices. Evaluate how social rank constrains characters' ambitions and relationships; examples include the social barriers faced by Gatsby. Assess whether the work conveys the system's rigidity and its emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of otherness / outsider status
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of Fitzgerald's characters are defined by their sense of 'otherness' arising from obscure origins, unclear identity, or indeterminate class status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at how novels make outsider status central to character motivation and social reception (e.g., Jay Gatsby as 'Mr. Nobody from Nowhere'). Consider ethnic, religious, regional, or class markers that render characters outsiders and how that shapes plot and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture of zeitgeist / generational voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald's fiction reflects the contemporary zeitgeist of the Jazz Age — an apolitical generation 'dedicated more than the last to the fear of poverty and the worship of success'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how convincingly a work embodies its era's attitudes (cynicism, aversion to political crusades, hedonism). Consider tone, thematic preoccupations, and whether the work functions as an interpreter of its generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic/ideational substance (alleged vacuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics alleged Fitzgerald's fiction 'lacked engagement with the salient socio-political issues of his time' and was seen as having 'few ideas to express.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the depth of intellectual or political engagement in the text. Does the work address broader social problems or remain narrowly focused on personal/psychological/material concerns? Note that Fitzgerald defended writing for an apolitical generation, which can contextualize apparent vacuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of autobiographical and appropriated material
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald often drew upon private correspondence, diary entries, and life experiences of others in his fiction (e.g., quoting letters, inserting wife's diary passages, borrowing friends' incidents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ethical and artistic implications of using real people's material: fidelity vs. appropriation, reactions of real-life subjects, and effects on authenticity. Examples show subjects felt 'queer' or requested excisions; some passages were restored later, indicating editorial/ethical complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative structure: series of disconnected scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald's style often used a series of disconnected scenes to convey plot developments, creating the impression of a railroad journey with vividly passing scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess effectiveness of vignette-style plotting: does the montage of scenes cohere thematically and emotionally? Consider pacing, transitions, and whether the technique enhances vividness or undermines narrative unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator as unifying device
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald often employed a narrator's device (in the style of Joseph Conrad) to unify disconnected scenes and imbue them with deeper meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the narrator's role in providing perspective, moral distance, or interpretive framing. Effective use should knit disparate scenes into a coherent moral/psychological whole; weak use can leave scenes disjointed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness of passing scenes / sensory imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptible vividness of passing scenes that 'blaze with life' — the technique of making fleeting moments strikingly alive for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge descriptive language, sensory detail, and the capacity of short episodes to create memorable impressions. Consider whether such vividness advances theme/character or serves only surface glamour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring relevance and contemporary resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Great Gatsby and other works resonate beyond their period because themes (status anxieties, social conflict) map onto present issues of race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a work's capacity to speak to later contexts: thematic universality, re-readability, and adaptability of themes to modern social concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability across media
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald's stories and novels have been adapted into many media formats (film, television, plays), with Gatsby adapted numerous times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cinematic or dramatic qualities—visual scenes, compact episodic structure, dialogue, and archetypal conflicts—that make a work suitable for adaptation. Consider whether adaptations highlight or distort original themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethos toward politics / apolitical posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald was largely indifferent to politics and did not believe fiction should be used as a political instrument; he wrote for an 'apolitical' generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing fiction, consider authorial stance toward political engagement: intentional avoidance may reflect thematic choices rather than failure. Contextualize apparent political disengagement within generational attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception versus technical gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporaries judged Fitzgerald to possess 'the best narrative gift of the century' yet argued he lacked engagement with larger social ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate assessments of craftsmanship (narrative gift, stylistic brilliance) from thematic ambition. A work may be technically excellent yet criticized for limited intellectual reach; reviews often balance these axes.
